definition: Twill is a weave in which interlacings step over by one yarn on each successive pick, producing diagonal lines called wales across the fabric.
explanation: Each warp end floats over or under at least two weft picks before interlacing, and the pattern shifts sideways every pick, so floats line up into a diagonal. A 2/2 twill shows equal warp and weft on the face; a 3/1 twill is warp-faced, showing mostly warp. The wale can run left or right, and reversing it at intervals creates herringbone. Longer floats and fewer interlacings than plain weave let yarns pack more closely, so twills can be denser, softer to drape and more resistant to tearing.
example: Examine the face of a pair of jeans: fine diagonal lines run upward, and the face is darker than the inside. Denim is typically a warp-faced twill with dyed warp and undyed weft, so the face shows mostly colored warp and the back mostly pale weft. Tracing one blue warp end under magnification shows it passing over three picks and under one before repeating.
caution: The diagonal line identifies twill structure, not fiber or quality. Twill does not guarantee durability, stretch or a particular weight. Some printed or brushed fabrics hide their structure, so inspect the reverse or ravel yarns to confirm. Wale direction and angle also depend on thread densities and yarn twist, not only on the weave plan.
deeper: Twill notation gives the number of picks a warp passes over, then under: 2/1, 2/2, 3/1 and so on, with a minimum repeat of three ends and three picks. The step, usually one yarn per pick, fixes the wale; changing thread density changes the wale angle, which is steep in gabardine. Fewer interlacings per unit area mean lower crimp and greater yarn mobility, so twills often drape more readily than plain weaves and allow higher thread densities. Research comparing weave structures reports that twill and satin fabrics differ from plain weave in stiffness, tensile and tear behavior, and one laundering study associated a cotton twill with lower microfiber release than satin, though fiber content was confounded.
origins: A twill needs at least three sheds, and therefore at least three shafts on a harness loom, which places it one step beyond plain weave in loom complexity. That extra control produced a large family of named fabrics distinguished by twill ratio, wale angle and finish, including drill, serge, gabardine and denim. Precise first dates for individual fabric names are not established here.

definition: Twist is the helical rotation of fibers or filaments around a yarn's axis, stated as turns per unit length plus a direction (S or Z), that holds staple fibers together.
explanation: Twist converts a loose strand of short fibers into a coherent yarn: when the yarn is pulled, the helically arranged fibers press inward on one another, and the resulting friction resists slippage. Direction is named by matching the slope of the surface fibers to the central stroke of a letter: fibers that follow the diagonal of a Z give Z twist, and those that follow an S give S twist. Twist level is quoted as turns per meter (tpm) or per inch (tpi). Plied yarns are usually twisted opposite to their singles, which balances torque and reduces snarling.
example: A knitter notices that a single Z-twisted yarn makes a jersey swatch that skews diagonally after washing, because the yarn's residual torque relaxes. Two of those singles are then plied together with S twist, giving a balanced two-ply yarn, and the new swatch stays square. The fiber and overall thickness are similar; the twist architecture is what changed.
caution: More twist is not always better. Strength rises with twist only up to an optimum, after which fibers lie too obliquely to carry load efficiently, and high twist also makes yarn harder, less bulky and more lively. A twist figure means little without the yarn's linear density, which is why twist multipliers are used. Continuous-filament yarns need little or no twist to hold together.
deeper: Finer yarns need more turns to reach the same surface helix angle, so twist is normalized with a multiplier. In metric terms the multiplier equals tpm multiplied by the square root of (tex divided by 1000), which is the same as tpm divided by the square root of metric count. In the English cotton-count convention, tpi equals the multiplier times the square root of Ne, and typical multipliers are roughly 3.0 to 3.6 for weft and knitting yarns, about 3.8 to 4.5 for warp yarns, and above 5 for crepe yarns. Twist is measured by untwisting a specimen of known length, either directly or by an untwist and retwist method.
origins: Twist direction is one of the first features recorded when a textile fragment is analyzed, because spinners in different traditions tended to favor one direction, so S or Z spin can hint at technique and origin. The letter convention is convenient because it does not depend on which end of the yarn the observer holds: a helix has the same handedness viewed from either end, so any two observers describe a given yarn the same way.

definition: A vat dye is an insoluble colorant that is chemically reduced to a soluble leuco form for application, then reoxidized inside the fiber to its insoluble colored form.
explanation: Vat dyes are pigments in their final state, so they cannot be applied directly. In the dyebath a reducing agent, commonly sodium dithionite under alkaline conditions, converts the dye to its leuco form, which is water-soluble and has affinity for cellulose. After the fiber absorbs the leuco dye, exposure to air or an oxidant regenerates the insoluble dye, trapping it within the fiber. Indigo is the best-known example and remains the dominant dye for denim.
example: A denim warp passes through an indigo leuco bath and emerges yellow-green, then turns blue within a minute or two in air as oxidation proceeds. Repeating dip and air cycles builds depth in the outer layers of each yarn, leaving the core paler. Later abrasion wears away the colored surface to reveal the lighter core, which is why washed denim fades in characteristic patterns.
caution: Vat dyes are a chemical class, not a natural-dye claim: indigo can come from plants, chemical synthesis or microbial biosynthesis, and the molecule is the same. The reducing step generates sulfite, sulfate and sulfide byproducts. Indigo on denim has limited rubbing fastness by design, so crocking onto light fabrics is expected. Other vat dyes can be very fast.
deeper: Indigo is a planar, poorly water-soluble molecule; reduction of its two carbonyl groups yields the leuco enolate, which is soluble at high pH. Leuco indigo has relatively low affinity for cotton, so rope and slasher dyeing use many short dips with oxidation between them, producing the ring-dyed yarn used for fading effects. Research to avoid sodium dithionite includes cyclodextrin inclusion complexes that raise indigo's solubility several-fold without chemical reduction. Industrial synthesis has historically relied on aniline, formaldehyde and hydrogen cyanide, and biosynthesis routes using flavin-containing monooxygenases are under development. Vat dyes also resist degradation in wastewater treatment, and one study found vat dyes more recalcitrant than reactive dyes to photocatalytic treatment. Beyond indigo, vat dyes can be added to cellulose dopes for spin dyeing.
origins: Indigo is among the oldest dyes, obtained historically from plants such as Indigofera species, and it remains central to cotton dyeing. The class name refers to the vessel, or vat, in which the reduced dyebath was traditionally prepared. Plant extraction gave way to chemical synthesis, which carries its own worker-safety and environmental concerns, and microbial production is now being explored as an alternative.
